analysis.one_liner: Lets the government directly negotiate prescription drug prices for Medicare.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices, backed by 35 senators, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the provision in Medicare law — added in 2003 — that forbids the government from negotiating drug prices directly with manufacturers. It would let the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services negotiate prices for drugs covered under Medicare's Part D benefit and set a reimbursement price structure. Today Medicare pays whatever prices private drug plans and manufacturers work out, with the government barred from stepping in.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of seniors and disabled Americans enrolled in Medicare's Part D drug benefit would gain if the government could negotiate lower prices directly, and taxpayers would gain because the federal government picks up a large share of Medicare drug costs. Medicare beneficiaries currently pay out-of-pocket amounts tied to prices set without any government negotiating power.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes subsection (i) of the Medicare law — the 'non-interference' provision from the 2003 Medicare Modernization Act that bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in price negotiations between drug makers and private Part D plans.

Once that bar is removed, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services could negotiate drug prices for the Part D benefit and institute a price structure for reimbursing covered drugs, giving the government the same kind of purchasing leverage other large buyers use.

The change would take effect immediately upon enactment, so negotiated prices would apply to drugs bought through Part D, where beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs and federal Medicare spending both depend on list prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face a customer with power to negotiate prices and set a reimbursement structure instead of accepting list prices. To the extent negotiated prices cut into manufacturer revenues, the industry argues this could reduce funds available for researching new drugs; private Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers would also see part of their negotiating role shift to the government.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a single provision — it removes the negotiating ban but says nothing about how hard CMS would push, what prices it would target, or what happens if manufacturers refuse to deal, leaving the real savings to depend entirely on how a future administration uses the power.

The strongest good-faith objection is that lower negotiated prices would cut manufacturer revenues, which the industry argues would mean less money for developing new medicines; supporters counter that the government already effectively sets drug prices through other programs like the VA and Medicaid without collapsing the pipeline.

The bill does not require any of the savings from negotiation to be passed to beneficiaries through lower out-of-pocket costs; unless Congress or CMS ties negotiated prices to what seniors pay, savings could flow mostly to the federal budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is simple and favorable to most people outside the drug industry: tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries and the federal budget face high drug prices largely because current law forbids the biggest purchaser in the country from negotiating, and this bill removes that bar at negligible budget cost. The honest costs are that savings depend entirely on how aggressively future administrations use the authority, and manufacturers' revenues — and possibly some drug development — would shrink. It is a narrow, unambiguous bill, not a comprehensive drug-pricing overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there — no committee vote, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on August 1, 2017, joined by 34 Democratic colleagues and one independent.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles Medicare legislation.
No further action of any kind was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off, because the 2003 ban on Medicare negotiating prices stays in place. So are the private Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers whose negotiating role is untouched, and the Senate's Republican leadership, which never had to take a recorded vote on the measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D intermediaries

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only non-Democrat

against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote during the Congress

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry (PhRMA and brand-name drug makers)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices, the position the bill would end

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats plus one independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill died without action in the Republican-chaired Finance Committee and the Republican-led Senate.

industries.note: The bill's entire effect is to let CMS negotiate prices and set a reimbursement structure for Part D drugs, replacing the current rule that the government must accept the prices that manufacturers and private plans work out. Manufacturer revenue on Medicare-covered drugs would be directly at stake.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: These intermediaries currently negotiate with drug makers on the government's behalf under the non-interference rule; direct government negotiation would shift part of that role to CMS. Their commissions and negotiating leverage would shrink, while beneficiaries' costs depend on the prices these intermediaries end up with.
